questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: That I would have the opportunity to live in an environment different from anything I’d experienced before.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
The host institution was very helpfull with orientation and sending material. But there are so many bureaucratic steps that even though they are very helpfull, it is quite overwhelming. I chose to live in a dorm, so I also had local students why could help translate, which was extremely helpfull. 
Although there’s a lot of paperwork to complete before and after arrival, it’s definitely manageable with a bit of patience and optimism.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The university had a helpful administration (International Center). Furthermore, each student is assigned a "student buddy" who can assist with translation. If you put yourself out there even a little, it’s easy to make local friends who are incredibly helpful with administrative matters!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I had no trouble finding housing. I got my preferred dorm, which I applied for, even though they don’t guarantee that you’ll get your first choice. I only heard of a few cases where students didn’t get their preferred dorm option. I’m not sure how housing works if you don’t go through the university, though.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: If you choose dorms through the university, none of them are located on campus, although one dorm can be a bit farther from the university than the others. I was very happy to live close to the university — and in the dorm that was also the closest to downtown. (I lived in Taishogun dorm)

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: If you’re used to living in dorms in Denmark, the facilities aren’t much different. However, due to cultural differences, there are many more rules and restrictions when living in university dorms in Japan. I didn’t find most of these rules limiting — they might seem a bit intimidating at first, but it’s really not that serious.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
It was super difficult and frustrating. The course registration process is a lottery system, so you’re not guaranteed to get your preferred courses. I ended up getting two out of the three courses I applied for, which led to a bit of a battle with the Merit Office at the University of Copenhagen to get pre-approval for the courses I had to take instead. It all worked out in the end, but it caused a lot of stress during the first month — which was really annoying.
If you study Political Science, you’re quite limited in that you can’t take courses outside the social sciences. Since the definition of “social sciences” can differ outside Europe, be prepared for a bit of back-and-forth between your host institution and your home university. It will most likely work out in the end — it did for me.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
You’re only allowed to take courses intended for international students, but most of these are language courses or ones I wasn’t able to get pre-approval for. You also don’t really know which courses will be offered until right before the semester begins.

Furthermore, there are laws in Japan requiring international students to take a certain number of class hours per semester, which you need to take into account. It can be a bit of a puzzle, but it’s really about “the art of the possible.” Again, it was stressful during the course registration period, but the host university’s administration was quite helpful and understanding. Unfortunately, Japan is a country where exceptions are rarely made and rules are meant to be followed.

In the end, though, everything worked out — and I think nine times out of ten, it will for others as well.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I had a very kind contact person at the University of Copenhagen’s Merit Office, for whom I was very thankful.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
I had checked which courses were offered in previous semesters, but I ended up choosing completely different ones when I arrived. This was either because the courses weren’t offered or because I learned from other students who had taken them before that they weren’t worth recommending — either due to the professor or the expected workload.

I wanted to take courses that allowed me to study something interesting but, more importantly, to enjoy my time abroad. You can study almost any subject anywhere in the world, but you can only truly experience life as an exchange student under these circumstances once or twice in your lifetime. Therefore, it was much more important for me to have time to enjoy myself than to be overwhelmed with academic work.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Keep your head up, and don’t let bureaucratic struggles ruin your experience. Studying abroad is a unique opportunity to do so much more than just study. Take courses you enjoy or that fit well with your schedule, but when choosing them, do so with the intention of giving yourself as much freedom as possible. There’s so much to explore outside the university.

And take a language course, even if you don’t get credit for it. Being able to communicate in the local language opens so many more doors!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Some of the courses were a bit laughable, while others were of the same standard — or even better — than those at KU. I’ve had both good and bad courses in Japan and Denmark, and you never really know what you’re getting into.

Classes in Japan usually have mandatory participation and weekly assignments that count toward your final grade. The weekly assignments are generally quite easy, and since they often make up between 20% and 40% of your final grade, they take some of the pressure off performing well during finals.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The BA courses were more comparable to first-year courses at KU or even to high school level, while the master’s courses were held to a higher standard.

The Japanese language course was perhaps the best class — with the best teacher — I’ve ever had throughout high school, my bachelor’s, and my master’s studies. I learned so much in just four months, and these classes were easily the most enjoyable part of going to university. 10/10 — highly recommended! Even though I didn’t receive any credits for them, they were absolutely worth it.
When will you ever have the chance to study a language for free in another country again?

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Classes were much more discussion-based and required active participation rather than one-way lectures. Overall, this format was OK, but the academic discussions were usually based more on personal experiences and interpretations rather than being anchored in academic reflection.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Globalization and Gender Issues (MA),  Lecture for Humanities (BA), Japanese Society (BA), Non-traditional Security (MA), Middel Eastern studies (MA), Japanese Ⅰ-1(Comprehensive)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Japanese Society (BA): Was a fun course for getting insight into Japan and some of the historical and cultural developments

Japanese I-1 (Comprehensive): As mentioned, this was perhaps the best class I’ve ever taken — with some of the best professors I’ve had.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: You’re required to pay for national health insurance and, generally, a bunch of other insurances through the university — but they’re quite cheap, in my opinion.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food, drinks, and experiences are so much cheaper than in Denmark. Go out and enjoy world-class food, drinks, and culture every day — all for a fraction of the price you’d pay back home.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The student association life at the university is on another level. There’s basically a club or society for everything imaginable, run by passionate students who truly care about their individual niches.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I was a member of the pottery club and the language exchange group — two great ways to meet local students and make local friends. It’s really a myth that you can’t make local friends; you just need to be open-minded :)

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Just join any club or society related to something you’re interested in learning about or already passionate about, and you’ll meet like-minded people.
Join a language exchange event and meet students who are interested in learning your language while teaching you Japanese.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Travel as much as you can — with friends and on your own. Japan is such an easily accessible country with kind people everywhere. Wherever you go, you’ll meet someone who wants to talk with you, have a drink with you, or show you around. Especially in smaller cities, people are often very excited to meet foreigners. Make the most of this privilege, and stay open-minded!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: There are a lot of local norms and unspoken rules. You aren’t expected to master them all or follow every single rule a Japanese person does, but you are expected to do the bare minimum. Learn a few words and customs, and you’ll get a long way very quickly. Be respectful and open-minded, and it won’t be difficult for you.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Just show up and be open-minded. It doesn’t really require more than that.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Many places only have information in Japanese, or the locals only speak Japanese. But that only makes it even more fun to try and communicate with local people — that’s why you’re going abroad anyway, right?

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The kind-heartedness of the locals - people from Kyoto (Kansai) are really unique

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: There’s so much more out there than the usual academic rush of studying in Copenhagen. Explore new cultures, eat amazing food, and meet incredible people. Travel as much and as far as you can.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don’t let immediate obstacles distract you from all the amazing experiences waiting for you. There are enough bureaucratic and academic challenges to keep you busy, but don’t let them overshadow what studying abroad is truly about. Do your assignments, fill out the forms, and finish your finals on time — then spend the rest enjoying life.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Making friends for life — it’s such a unique experience being abroad, with both other international students and local friends.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Going home again

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
